newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Channel tunnel blaze inquiry to blame arson.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Channel tunnel blaze inquiry to blame arson.

text.p: Last year's blaze in the Channel Tunnel was started by arson, a French judicial inquiry to be published next week is expected to rule, sources close to the investigation told Reuters on Friday.

The blaze in the tunnel connecting Britain and France on November 18 started on a freight wagon, caused 200 million pounds ($328 million) of damage and a number of truck drivers on the train were taken to hospital.
"It seems that we can now exclude the hypothesis that is was purely accidental," a source close to the French investigation told Reuters in Paris on Friday.
This was mirrored in comments made to Reuters by another source involved in some of the key British investigations.
"We've heard through unofficial channels that once the report is published, it will clearly indicate a human cause -- arson," the British source said.
The fire, which happened at the French Calais end of the tunnel, has already been examined in separate reports by operator Eurotunnel Plc and the Channel Tunnel Safety Authority.

But investigating the cause of the fire has been the sole remit of the French judicial inquiry. Eurotunnel and the Safety Authority have already ruled out a technical or mechanical failure as the cause.

The French state prosecutor leading the investigation will hold a news conference next week to report his preliminary findings, it was confirmed. But Gerald Lesigne, prosecutor for Boulogne-sur-Mer, would not comment on the arson speculation.
Eurotunnel remained noncommittal when asked whether it had been given advance notice of the French inquiry outcome.
"Until the report comes out we can't be certain," said a Eurotunnel spokeswoman.
Next week Eurotunnel will also find out whether or not it will have to redesign its wagons to make them safer.
The Anglo-French Intergovernmental Commission is due to give its final judgement on the fire after having digested this week's report from the Safety Authority.
The crucial issue for Eurotunnel is whether the Commission will back the Safety Authority report in not calling for a redesign of the controversial open-sided freight wagons.
Controversy raged earlier this week when the wagon design was cleared despite continued safety reservations being raised by fire chiefs.

Jeremy Beech, head of the Kent Fire Brigade, who said the current wagon design created a "blow-torch effect" after the blaze last year, has publicly disagreed with the decision of the Safety Authority on this, despite being a member of it.
It is understood that Beech, whose team fought the blaze, has met with John Prescott, Britain's deputy prime minister and head of the transport and environment ministry, to discuss his concerns.

Getting clearance from the Commission to resume freight services and avoiding a costly redesign of wagons are key to Eurotunnel as it prepares for an even bigger battle -- persuading shareholders and bankers to back its nine billion pound debt restructuring survival plan this summer.
